## Introduction

A C program consists of preprocessor directives, global declarations, and functions. Every C program must have a main() function — that's where execution begins. Understanding the structure is the first step to writing C programs.
## Key Concepts

- Preprocessor directives: #include <stdio.h> includes the standard I/O library
- main() function: the entry point of every C program — execution starts here
- Statements: each statement ends with a semicolon (;)
- Curly braces { } define blocks of code
- return 0; indicates successful program termination
- printf() prints output to the screen; scanf() reads input from the keyboard
- Comments: // single line, /* multi line */ — ignored by the compiler

## Important Formulas

- `Program structure: #include → global vars → functions → main()`
- `printf format: printf("format string", variables);`
- `scanf format: scanf("format string", &variables);  (note the & for address)`

## Comparison Tables

### Common printf/scanf Format Specifiers

| Specifier | Data Type | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| %d | int | printf("%d", 42); |
| %f | float | printf("%f", 3.14); |
| %c | char | printf("%c", 'A'); |
| %s | string (char array) | printf("%s", name); |
| %lf | double | printf("%lf", 3.14159); |
| %% | literal % | printf("100%%"); |

> Forgetting the & in scanf is a common error: scanf("%d", &num), NOT scanf("%d", num).

## Code Examples

### Your First C Program — Hello World with Input

```c
#include <stdio.h>  // preprocessor directive

int main() {
    // Variable declaration
    int age;
    char name[50];

    // Input
    printf("Enter your name: ");
    scanf("%s", name);  // no & needed for strings (array name is already an address)

    printf("Enter your age: ");
    scanf("%d", &age);  // & needed for int

    // Output
    printf("\nHello, %s!\n", name);
    printf("You are %d years old.\n", age);

    return 0;  // success
}
```

This program asks for the user's name and age, then prints a greeting. Note: scanf needs & for int but not for string (array name is already a pointer). The \n creates a new line.


## Summary

A C program consists of preprocessor directives, global declarations, and functions. Every C program must have a main() function — that's where execution begins. Understanding the structure is the first step to writing C programs.

## Introduction

C has several built-in data types for storing different kinds of data: int for integers, float for decimals, char for characters, and more. Operators perform operations on variables and values — arithmetic, relational, logical, and assignment operators.
## Key Concepts

- int: whole numbers (4 bytes, range -2³¹ to 2³¹-1). Modifiers: short, long, unsigned.
- float: single-precision decimal (4 bytes, ~7 digits). double: double-precision (8 bytes, ~15 digits).
- char: single character (1 byte). Stored as ASCII integer internally.
- Arithmetic operators: +, -, *, /, % (modulo — remainder of division)
- Relational operators: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= (return 1 for true, 0 for false)
- Logical operators: && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT)
- Assignment operators: =, +=, -=, *=, /=, %=
- Increment/decrement: ++ (add 1), -- (subtract 1). Pre: ++x (increment then use). Post: x++ (use then increment).

## Important Formulas

- `Size: int=4 bytes, float=4 bytes, double=8 bytes, char=1 byte`
- `Integer division: 7/2 = 3 (not 3.5!) — both operands are int, so result is int`
- `Modulo: 7 % 2 = 1 (remainder of 7÷2)`
- `Type casting: (float)7/2 = 3.5 — cast one operand to float before division`

## Comparison Tables

### C Data Types

| Type | Size (bytes) | Range | Format Specifier |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| int | 4 | -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 | %d |
| unsigned int | 4 | 0 to 4,294,967,295 | %u |
| short | 2 | -32,768 to 32,767 | %hd |
| long | 4 or 8 | platform-dependent | %ld |
| float | 4 | ±3.4×10³⁸ (~7 digits) | %f |
| double | 8 | ±1.7×10³⁰⁸ (~15 digits) | %lf |
| char | 1 | -128 to 127 (or 0-255 unsigned) | %c |

> Sizes may vary by platform. Use sizeof(type) to check on your system.
### Operator Precedence (high to low)

| Operator | Description | Associativity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| () [] -> . | Function call, array, member | Left to right |
| ! ++ -- - (type) | Unary operators | Right to left |
| * / % | Multiplication, division, modulo | Left to right |
| + - | Addition, subtraction | Left to right |
| < <= > >= == != | Relational | Left to right |
| && | Logical AND | Left to right |
| || | Logical OR | Left to right |
| = += -= etc. | Assignment | Right to left |

> Higher precedence operators are evaluated first. Use parentheses to override.

## Code Examples

### Operators in Action

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a = 10, b = 3;

    // Arithmetic
    printf("a + b = %d\n", a + b);   // 13
    printf("a - b = %d\n", a - b);   // 7
    printf("a * b = %d\n", a * b);   // 30
    printf("a / b = %d\n", a / b);   // 3 (integer division!)
    printf("a %% b = %d\n", a % b);  // 1 (remainder)

    // Type casting
    printf("(float)a / b = %f\n", (float)a / b);  // 3.333333

    // Relational (return 1 or 0)
    printf("a > b: %d\n", a > b);    // 1 (true)
    printf("a == b: %d\n", a == b);  // 0 (false)

    // Logical
    printf("(a > 5) && (b < 5): %d\n", (a > 5) && (b < 5));  // 1 (both true)
    printf("(a < 5) || (b < 5): %d\n", (a < 5) || (b < 5));  // 1 (one is true)

    // Increment/decrement
    int x = 5;
    printf("x++ = %d\n", x++);  // 5 (print then increment)
    printf("x = %d\n", x);      // 6 (now incremented)
    printf("++x = %d\n", ++x);  // 7 (increment then print)

    return 0;
}
```

Note that 10/3 = 3 (integer division — the decimal part is truncated). To get a decimal result, cast one operand to float: (float)10/3 = 3.33. Also note the difference between x++ (post) and ++x (pre).

codeExamples.explanation: swapByValue receives copies of x and y — swapping the copies doesn't affect the originals. swapByReference receives the addresses (&x, &y) and swaps the values at those addresses — the originals ARE changed.

codeExamples.title: Recursion — Factorial
codeExamples.explanation: Recursion has two parts: (1) the base case (n <= 1 → return 1) that stops the recursion, and (2) the recursive case (n * factorial(n-1)) that reduces the problem. Without a base case, recursion never stops — stack overflow!

practiceQuestions.question: What is required to prevent infinite recursion?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A base case is a condition that stops the recursion (e.g., if (n <= 1) return 1;). Without it, the function calls itself forever, eventually causing a stack overflow.

practiceQuestions.question: How are arrays passed to functions in C?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Arrays are always passed by reference in C. When you pass an array name, it decays to a pointer to the first element. Changes made inside the function affect the original array.

# Programming in C — Quick Revision

**Subject code:** R23CP1401  
**Semester:** 2  
**Credits:** 5  

## Unit 1: C Basics and Program Structure (15%)
### Structure of a C Program
A C program consists of preprocessor directives, global declarations, and functions. Every C program must have a main() function — that's where execution begins. Understanding the structure is the first step to writing C programs.

**Formulas:**
- `Program structure: #include → global vars → functions → main()`
- `printf format: printf("format string", variables);`
- `scanf format: scanf("format string", &variables);  (note the & for address)`

### Data Types, Variables, and Operators
C has several built-in data types for storing different kinds of data: int for integers, float for decimals, char for characters, and more. Operators perform operations on variables and values — arithmetic, relational, logical, and assignment operators.

**Formulas:**
- `Size: int=4 bytes, float=4 bytes, double=8 bytes, char=1 byte`
- `Integer division: 7/2 = 3 (not 3.5!) — both operands are int, so result is int`
- `Modulo: 7 % 2 = 1 (remainder of 7÷2)`

## Unit 2: Control Structures (20%)
### Decision Making — if-else and switch
Control structures allow a program to make decisions and repeat actions. The if-else statement executes different code based on a condition. The switch statement selects one of many code blocks based on a value. These are the building blocks of logic in C.

**Formulas:**
- `if: if (condition) { /* code */ }`
- `if-else: if (condition) { /* A */ } else { /* B */ }`
- `switch: switch (var) { case 1: ...; break; case 2: ...; break; default: ...; }`

### Loops — for, while, and do-while
Loops repeat a block of code multiple times. The 'for' loop is used when you know the number of iterations. The 'while' loop checks the condition BEFORE executing (may run 0 times). The 'do-while' loop checks AFTER executing (runs at least once). Loops are essential for processin...

**Formulas:**
- `for: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { /* runs n times */ }`
- `while: while (condition) { /* runs while true */ }`
- `do-while: do { /* runs at least once */ } while (condition);`

## Unit 3: Functions and Arrays (25%)
### Functions — Definition, Declaration, and Call
A function is a reusable block of code that performs a specific task. Functions help organize code, avoid repetition, and make programs modular. C programs are collections of functions that call each other. The main() function is where execution starts.

**Formulas:**
- `Declaration: returnType functionName(paramType param);`
- `Definition: returnType functionName(paramType param) { /* code */ return value; }`
- `Call: functionName(arguments);`
